sections.b: Mark 13 is probably the earliest written form of the speech on the Mount of Olives, which Matthew 24–25 and Luke 21 expand. Mark names its private hearers, Peter, James, John and Andrew (13:3), keeps the warnings of trial in the speech (13:9–13), adds that the good news must first reach all the nations (13:10), makes the abomination a masculine "he" standing where he must not, with an aside to the reader (13:14), and ends with a short parable of a doorkeeper and the four watches of the night (13:33–37). Its refrain is "watch out" (13:5, 9, 23, 33) and "stay awake" (13:35, 37), and the passion that follows tests these very listeners at once. Chapter 13 is also the main evidence in the debate over whether Mark was written before or after the Temple fell in AD 70.

common: Most scholars think Mark wrote between AD 65 and 75, and that chapter 13 reflects the years of the Jewish War.
uncommon: Gerd Theissen argued that an older warning leaflet from the Caligula crisis of AD 40 lies behind Mark 13:14–20.

sections.h: "Standing where he must not" in Mark
sections.b: Mark 13:14 makes Daniel's "abomination of desolation" (a neuter noun in Greek) stand as a masculine "he," and it does not name Daniel (the oldest manuscripts lack "spoken of by Daniel the prophet"). The aside "the one who reads this should think about what it means" therefore speaks to the reader of Mark. Proposed identifications include the emperor Gaius, who in AD 40 ordered his statue set up in the Temple; the Zealot leaders who occupied the Temple in 67–68; Titus and his soldiers in AD 70; and a future Antichrist like the "man of lawlessness" (2 Thessalonians 2:3–4).
sections.refs: Mark 13:14; Daniel 9:27; Daniel 11:31; Daniel 12:11; Matthew 24:15; 2 Thessalonians 2:3–4

sections.h: The Son of Man in Mark 13 and 14
sections.b: Mark speaks of the Son of Man "coming in clouds, with much power and glory" to gather his chosen from the farthest edge of the earth to the farthest edge of the sky (13:26–27), and Jesus tells the high priest that he will see the Son of Man "sitting at the Power's right hand and coming with the clouds of the sky" (14:62). Both draw on Daniel 7:13. Most Christian readers take them of Christ's return; some scholars, such as N. T. Wright, read them as his vindication before God, shown in the fall of the Temple. Mark has no "immediately" before the cosmic signs (13:24), and he insists that no one, not even the Son, knows the day (13:32).

In Mark 14:3–9 an unnamed woman breaks an alabaster jar of pure nard and pours it on Jesus' head in the house of Simon, the man with skin disease. Prophets anointed kings on the head; here a woman anoints the Messiah two days before he is mocked as "King of the Jews." Jesus defends her against those who call it waste and says she has anointed his body ahead of time for burial, a meaning sharpened when the women who come to anoint his body on Sunday find the tomb empty (16:1–6). He promises she will be remembered wherever the good news is told. John 12:1–8 names her as Mary of Bethany; Luke 7:36–50 tells a different anointing.
sections.refs: Mark 14:3–9; Mark 16:1; Matthew 26:6–13; John 12:1–8; Luke 7:36–50; 1 Samuel 10:1

sections.b: Mark 14:22–25 is the shortest account of Jesus' words: "Take it" and "This is my body"; "This is my blood of the covenant. It is being poured out for many." It has no "eat," no "so that sins can be forgiven" (Matthew), and no "do this in remembrance of me" (Paul and Luke); the oldest manuscripts also lack "new" before covenant. The words echo the blood of the covenant at Sinai (Exodus 24:8) and the servant who bore the sin of many (Isaiah 53:12), and Jesus vows not to drink wine again until he drinks it new in the kingdom of God. The Where Christians differ cards at Matthew 26:26–28 set out how the churches understand "This is my body."

Mark gives no motive for Judas. He is "one of the Twelve" (14:10, 20, 43), the phrase repeated as if Mark could not get over it. He goes to the chief priests, who promise him silver; he finds the right moment; he gives the agreed sign, a kiss, and greets Jesus as "Rabbi" (14:44–45). Mark tells nothing of his end. Jesus' word holds both God's plan and Judas's guilt: the Son of Man goes as it is written, "But woe to the man through whom the Son of Man is handed over!" (14:21).

sections.h: Peter's denial and "and Peter" in Mark
sections.b: Mark, the Gospel that tradition ties most closely to Peter, is also the hardest on him. He insists he will never deny Jesus (14:29–31), sleeps in Gethsemane, where Jesus calls him by his old name, "Simon" (14:37), follows from far back and warms himself at the fire, then denies Jesus three times, the last time with curses, before the rooster crows twice (14:66–72). Mark sets the denial around Jesus' trial, so that Jesus' "I am" and Peter's "I do not know this man" are heard together. Peter's tears are his last scene; the young man at the tomb then sends the news to "his disciples, and Peter" (16:7), a word of restoration.
sections.refs: Mark 14:29–31; Mark 14:37; Mark 14:54; Mark 14:66–72; Mark 16:7; 1 Corinthians 15:5

sections.b: Mark keeps two of Jesus' Aramaic prayers at the end of his life. In Gethsemane he prays "Abba, Father" (14:36), the family word for father, which Greek-speaking Christians kept in their own prayers (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6); it does not mean "Daddy," as is often said. On the cross he cries "Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?", the first line of Psalm 22 in Aramaic (15:34), which bystanders mistake for a call to Elijah. Matthew gives the cry in a more Hebrew form, "Eli, Eli."
sections.refs: Mark 14:36; Mark 15:34–35; Psalm 22:1; Matthew 27:46; Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6

sections.b: Mark tells the crucifixion simply and by the clock: crucified at the third hour, darkness from the sixth, death at the ninth (15:25, 33–34). The charge, "The King of the Jews," hangs above him; two bandits hang at his right and left, the places James and John had asked for (10:37). Passers-by, priests and bandits mock him in words that echo Psalm 22. He refuses wine mixed with myrrh, prays the opening of Psalm 22 in Aramaic, gives a loud cry and dies quickly enough to surprise Pilate. A Roman centurion is the first human being in Mark to call him God's Son (15:39).

sections.h: God's Son in Mark's last chapters
sections.b: Mark 13:32 is the one place where Jesus calls himself simply "the Son" beside "the Father," above the angels, and yet says he does not know the day. Before the high priest he answers "I am" to "the Son of the Blessed One" (14:61–62). At his death, as the curtain is torn, a Roman centurion says, "This man really was God's Son!" (15:39), the first human confession of it in Mark and the climax of the book that began by naming him Son of God (1:1, 11). Whether the soldier meant "the Son of God" or "a son of a god" is debated; Mark's meaning is clear.
sections.refs: Mark 1:1; Mark 1:11; Mark 9:7; Mark 13:32; Mark 14:61–62; Mark 15:39

sections.h: Mark's last word on the Temple
sections.b: Jesus leaves the Temple and foretells that not one stone will be left on a stone (13:1–2). False witnesses claim he said he would destroy "this sanctuary that human hands made" and build another "that no hands made" (14:58), using the Greek Bible's word for idols; the taunt returns at the cross (15:29). When Jesus dies, the sanctuary curtain is torn in two from top to bottom (15:38), the same verb Mark used for the heavens torn open at his baptism (1:10). Readers have seen in it judgment on the Temple, an opened way to God, and the revelation of God in the crucified one.
sections.refs: Mark 13:1–2; Mark 14:58; Mark 15:29; Mark 15:38; Mark 1:10; Hebrews 10:19–20

sections.b: Mark's Pilate asks only, "So you are the King of the Jews?" (15:2), is amazed at Jesus' silence, knows the chief priests acted from jealousy, and tries to free him by a Passover custom. When the crowd, stirred by the priests, demands Barabbas and shouts "Crucify him!", Pilate wants to keep the crowd happy, frees Barabbas, has Jesus whipped and hands him over (15:15). Later he checks with the centurion that Jesus is really dead and gives the body to Joseph (15:44–45). Mark has no hand-washing and no warning dream; his Pilate chooses public order over justice.

sections.h: The women who stayed, in Mark
sections.b: In Mark 15:40–41 the reader learns for the first time that women had followed Jesus and served him in Galilee and come with him to Jerusalem: Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the younger and Joses, Salome and many others. The men have fled; the women watch his death, see where he is laid (15:47), and come first to the empty tomb (16:1–8). Mark uses for them the words of discipleship, "follow" and "serve," the second the word Jesus used of his own mission (10:45). An unnamed woman also anoints Jesus and is promised lasting memory (14:9).

Mark names Mary Magdalene first among the women who watch the crucifixion (15:40), who see where Jesus is laid (15:47), and who come to the tomb with spices and hear that he has been raised (16:1–8). The Longer Ending adds that the risen Jesus appeared first to her and that she had been freed from seven demons (16:9), drawing on Luke 8:2 and John 20:11–18, and that the disciples did not believe her (16:10–11).

Mark's account (16:1–8) is the oldest narrative of the empty tomb. Three women who saw Jesus die and saw where he was laid come at sunrise with spices, find the large stone rolled back, and meet a young man in white who says: "You are looking for Jesus the Nazarene, the one who was crucified. He has been raised. He isn't here." He sends them to tell the disciples and Peter that Jesus is going ahead of them to Galilee. In the oldest manuscripts the Gospel ends with their frightened silence, telling no appearance; the Longer Ending (16:9–20) summarizes appearances known from the other Gospels and the ascension.

Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, the two oldest manuscripts that contain the end of Mark, end Mark at 16:8, "for they were afraid"; so do the Sinaitic Syriac and the oldest Armenian and Georgian manuscripts, and Eusebius and Jerome said most Greek copies they knew did the same. Most later manuscripts add the Longer Ending (16:9–20), known by about AD 170–180 to Tatian and Irenaeus. One Old Latin manuscript has only a two-sentence Shorter Ending; several later Greek manuscripts have both. Codex Washington adds a further exchange after 16:14, the Freer Logion. Most scholars judge that Mark wrote none of these endings and debate whether he meant to stop at 16:8 or his ending was lost.

common: Most scholars hold that Mark 16:9–20 was added in the second century.
uncommon: A minority, including some defenders of the Byzantine text, hold that Mark himself wrote 16:9–20.

sections.h: Is the Longer Ending of Mark Scripture?
sections.b: Mark 16:9–20 is a test case for how churches relate the canon to the history of the text. Catholic teaching receives it as canonical because it has long been read in the church and stands in the Latin Vulgate, whatever its author; the Orthodox read it in the Sunday resurrection Gospels at Matins; Anglicans and evangelicals are divided, many printing it with a note and declining to build doctrine on it alone. The Where Christians differ card at Mark 16 sets out the views.

The Longer Ending's commission joins faith and baptism: "The one who has believed and been baptized will be saved. The one who has refused to believe will be condemned." Churches that teach that baptism is necessary for salvation cite it (the Catholic Catechism, Luther's Small Catechism, Churches of Christ); others point out that the second half condemns unbelief, not lack of baptism (Reformed and Baptist teaching). Its place in a later ending is also weighed. See the Where Christians differ card at Mark 16.

sections.h: The Spirit in Mark's last chapters
sections.b: Jesus promises disciples on trial that "the Holy Spirit" will speak through them (13:11), a promise kept in Acts. The Longer Ending promises signs to those who believe, among them speaking "in new tongues" (16:17), a link with Pentecost (Acts 2:4). Christians differ on whether such signs continue today: see the Where Christians differ cards at Mark 16 and Matthew 10.

The Longer Ending promises that signs will follow believers: driving out demons in Jesus' name, new tongues, taking up snakes, drinking poison unharmed, and healing the sick by laying on hands. Nearly all have parallels in Acts (Acts 28:3–6, Paul's viper on Malta). A small movement of Appalachian Holiness churches, begun by George Went Hensley in the early 1900s, handles venomous snakes in worship on the strength of this verse; most churches read it as a promise of protection in unsought danger, not a command, and many weigh its place in a later ending.

sections.h: Taken up, in the Longer Ending of Mark
sections.b: Mark 16:19 says that after speaking with the Eleven, "the Lord Jesus" was taken up into heaven and sat down at God's right hand, using the Greek Bible's verb for Elijah's going up (2 Kings 2:11) and the words of Psalm 110:1. Irenaeus quoted this verse as from the end of Mark about AD 180. Mark 1:1–16:8 itself has no ascension, but Jesus told the high priest that he would be seen "sitting at the Power's right hand" (14:62).

sections.h: Jesus before the council in Mark
sections.b: Mark 14:53–65 sets a night hearing in the high priest's house before "all the chief priests, elders and scribes," the whole Sanhedrin. False witnesses cannot agree, as the Law required (Deuteronomy 19:15); the high priest then asks Jesus directly whether he is the Messiah, and Jesus' "I am" with the words of Psalm 110 and Daniel 7 is judged blasphemy. At dawn the council hands him over to Pilate (15:1). Historians debate whether this was a formal trial, which would break the rules later written in the Mishnah, or a hearing to prepare a charge for Rome. A council member, Joseph of Arimathea, later buries Jesus (15:43).

In the oldest manuscripts Mark ends at 16:8: the women run from the empty tomb and say nothing to anyone, "for they were afraid." Later Christians supplied endings: a two-sentence Shorter Ending, the Longer Ending of 16:9–20 that most Bibles print, and, in one manuscript, a further saying after 16:14 (the Freer Logion). Most scholars think Mark wrote none of them; they debate whether he meant to end at 16:8, as many literary readers hold, or whether his last page was lost. The evidence is set out on the chapter page for Mark 16.

sections.h: Mark 13 and the date of the Gospel
sections.b: The speech on the Mount of Olives is the main evidence for when Mark wrote. Those who date Mark before AD 70 point to the lack of detail about the city's fall and to links with the Caligula crisis of AD 40; those who date it just after point to the fulfilled prophecy of the Temple's destruction and to the aside "the one who reads this should think about what it means" (13:14). Most scholars settle on 65–75.
